The density formula gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$ exactly when $\int 1_{\{p_\theta=0\}}p_0\,d\mu=0$; Tonelli [F4] makes this condition measurable in $\theta$. On this measurable set, the extended log-density parts defining $K(\theta)$ are product-measurable and Tonelli makes their section integrals measurable; outside it the KL value is $+\infty$ by [F2]. Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta)$ and $B_\epsilon$ are measurable. By [F1], for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$, $\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)} =-\bigl(K(\theta)-K^*\bigr)\ge-\epsilon.$ Both KL values are finite on this set, so [F2] makes the log ratio integrable.

For each fixed $\theta$ in this full-prior subset of $B_\epsilon$, $L_i^\theta:=\log(p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i))$ are IID integrable real variables: the data are IID and [F6] preserves independence under the measurable log-ratio map. By [F5], $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n L_i^\theta \longrightarrow-\bigl(K(\theta)-K^*\bigr)\ge-\epsilon \quad P_0^\infty\text{-almost surely}.$ The event of this convergence is jointly measurable in $(\theta,X_1,X_2,\ldots)$. Tonelli [F4] applied to the indicator of its failure, under $\Pi|_{B_\epsilon}\times P_0^\infty$, therefore gives a $P_0^\infty$-full event on which convergence holds for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$.

For fixed $n$, the finite product measures $\mu^n$ and $P_0^n$ exist by [F17]. The nonnegative jointly measurable likelihood $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)$ is product-measurable by [F15] and integrates to one over $\mu^n$ for every $\theta$, by [F16] and repeated integration. Tonelli [F4] therefore gives $\int_{\mathsf X^n}\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)\, \Pi(d\theta)\,\mu^n(dx_{1:n})=1.$ Let $Z_n(x_{1:n})=\int_\Theta\prod_i p_\theta(x_i)\Pi(d\theta)$. By [F11], $Z_n<\infty$ $\mu^n$-almost everywhere. The sample vector has law $P_0^n$ by [F9]. Its product density relative to $\mu^n$ is $\prod_i p_0(x_i)$: repeated Tonelli gives this density's rectangle formula, and [F10] identifies the resulting measure with $P_0^n$. Therefore $Z_n<\infty$ $P_0^n$-almost surely.

For $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$, finite KL gives $P_0\ll P_\theta$ by [F2], so $p_\theta(X_i)>0$ almost surely for each coordinate. The coordinate products are measurable by [F15]; Tonelli [F4] applied to the indicator of a zero likelihood shows that, for $P_0^n$-almost every sample, $p_\theta(X_i)>0$ for every $i$ for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$. Since $\Pi(B_\epsilon)>0$, $Z_n>0$. Finally, $p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$ is finite and positive $P_0$-almost surely, so the relative denominator $D_n$ is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely.

Fix $\alpha>\epsilon$ and choose $\alpha'$ with $\epsilon<\alpha'<\alpha$. On the event from step 1.2, for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta\in B_\epsilon$ the log likelihood average is eventually greater than $-\alpha'$. Therefore $e^{n\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_{\theta^*}(X_i)} \ge e^{n(\alpha-\alpha')}\longrightarrow+\infty.$ Fatou's lemma [F14] for the nonnegative integrands gives $\liminf_{n\to\infty}e^{n\alpha}D_n \ge\int_{B_\epsilon}\liminf_{n\to\infty} e^{n\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_{\theta^*}(X_i)} \,\Pi(d\theta)=+\infty,$ since $\Pi(B_\epsilon)>0$. Hence $D_n\ge e^{-n\alpha}$ eventually.
Steps 1.3–2.2 establish finite-positive evidence, and step 2.2 establishes the eventual exponential lower bound asserted in the Statement.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Pi$ be a prior probability on $\Theta$, let $B_\epsilon$ be the
measurable relative KL neighborhood from
[[def-kl-projection-set-and-relative-kl-neighborhoods]], and suppose
$\Pi(B_\epsilon)>0$. Assume the log likelihood ratios
$\log(p_\theta/p_{\theta^*})$ are $P_0$-integrable for $\Pi$-almost every
$\theta\in B_\epsilon$. For
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_{\theta^*}(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta),$$
every $\alpha>\epsilon$ satisfies
$$D_n\ge e^{-n\alpha}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$, $P_0$-almost surely. Under the stated
jointly measurable dominated model, $D_n$ is also finite and positive
$P_0^n$-almost surely for each $n$.

Under the setup of [[def-likelihood-tilted-measure-at-kl-projection]] and
[[lem-likelihood-tilted-measure-is-sigma-finite]], for each $\theta$ and
integer $n\ge1$, the sigma-finite product measure $Q_\theta^n$ exists and
has density
$$\prod_{i=1}^n r_\theta(x_i),\qquad r_\theta(x):=\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)},$$
relative to $P_0^n$. Ratios are zero where $p_{\theta^*}=0$, as in the
likelihood-tilt definition.

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is

$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an independent sequence of random elements, and
let $\mathcal T(X_n:n\in\mathbb N)$ be its tail sigma-algebra. Then every event
$A\in\mathcal T(X_n:n\in\mathbb N)$ satisfies
$$\mathbb P(A)\in\{0,1\}.$$

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
Every characteristic function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb R$ satisfies $\varphi(0)=1$, $|\varphi(t)|\le1$, $\varphi(-t)=\overline{\varphi(t)}$, and is uniformly continuous on $\mathbb R$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

derivations.claim: Let $M=\sup_{n\ge0}S_n$, a measurable $[0,+\infty]$-valued random variable. For each $m\ge1$, removing the first $m$ increments changes later partial sums only by the finite number $S_m$, and the removed partial sums form a finite set. Consequently $\{M=+\infty\}=\{\sup_{k\ge0}\sum_{i=m+1}^{m+k}X_i=+\infty\}$ belongs to $\sigma(X_{m+1},X_{m+2},\ldots)$. It is a tail event, so its probability is zero or one.

Suppose its probability were zero. Then $M$ is finite almost surely. Define $M'=\sup_{k\ge0}\sum_{i=2}^{k+1}X_i$, which is also finite almost surely and has the same law as $M$: for every real $b$, the event that the supremum is at most $b$ is the decreasing intersection of the corresponding finite-prefix events, whose probabilities agree by the IID hypothesis. The variable $M'$ is independent of $X_1$ by independence of their coordinate sigma-algebras. Decomposing the supremum according to whether the empty partial sum is used gives $M=\max(0,X_1+M')$ almost surely. On null exceptional sets replace $M$ and $M'$ by zero if needed, without changing their laws or these almost-sure assertions.

Put $A=\max(0,M'+X_1)$ and $B=M'$, so $A$ and $B$ are finite nonnegative variables with the same law. The map $u\mapsto\max(0,u)$ is one-Lipschitz and $B\ge0$, hence $|A-B|\le|X_1|$. For each positive integer $K$, equality in law gives $\mathbb E[\min(A,K)-\min(B,K)]=0$. The difference converges almost surely to $A-B$ and has absolute value at most $|A-B|\le|X_1|$. Dominated convergence therefore yields $\mathbb E(A-B)=0$, without requiring either $A$ or $B$ to have finite expectation.

The identity $A-B=X_1+R$, where $R=(-B-X_1)^+$ and $u^+=\max(u,0)$, gives $0\le R\le|X_1|$. Centering and step 2.1 imply $\mathbb ER=0$, so $R=0$ almost surely. Thus $B+X_1=A$ almost surely and $B+X_1$ has the same law as $B$. Independence now gives $\varphi_B(t)\varphi_{X_1}(t)=\varphi_B(t)$ for every real $t$.

Continuity and $\varphi_B(0)=1$ supply $\delta>0$ such that $\varphi_B(t)\ne0$ for $|t|<\delta$. Step 2.2 then gives $\varphi_{X_1}(t)=1$ on this interval. Choose a positive integer $q$ with $1/q<\delta$. For every integer $k\ge q$, taking real parts gives $\mathbb E[1-\cos(X_1/k)]=0$, so $\cos(X_1/k)=1$ almost surely. Intersecting these countably many probability-one events, fix a resulting value $x$ of $X_1$. If $x\ne0$, some $k\ge q$ has $0<|x|/k<2\pi$, contradicting $\cos(x/k)=1$. Therefore $X_1=0$ almost surely, contrary to the hypothesis.

The zero-probability alternative in step 1.1 is impossible, so $M=+\infty$ almost surely. Each finite prefix has finite maximum, and hence removing it preserves an infinite supremum. Thus the limsup of the partial sums is also $+\infty$ almost surely.

Moreover $E_0[Y^21_{\{Y\le b\}}]=c\int_e^b(\log y)^{-2}dy=O(b/(\log b)^2)$: split the integral at $\sqrt b$, bound the first part by $\sqrt b$, and the second by $4b/(\log b)^2$. The variance of $\sum_{i=1}^nY_i1_{\{Y_i\le b_n\}}$ is at most $O(nb_n/(\log b_n)^2)$ by independence. Dividing this bound by $(n/\log n)^2$ gives $O(b_n/n)\to0$. Put $\epsilon_j=N_j^{-1}$. Thus $\epsilon_j>0$ and $\epsilon_j\to0$; these constants depend only on the true law, not the realized observations. By [F5], $T_j\le N_j$ eventually almost surely. Also $T_j\to\infty$ almost surely, since finitely many finite partial sums cannot exceed arbitrarily large levels.

For any selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ with finite contrast, the relative
contrast on $B_\epsilon$ satisfies
$$K(\theta)-K^*=-\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}$$
whenever the displayed log ratio is integrable. This definition allows
$\Theta^*$ to contain multiple parameters and does not assert that the
posterior selects one of them.

Fix a selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ as in
[[def-kl-projection-set-and-relative-kl-neighborhoods]]. Since its KL value is
finite, $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. For each $\theta\in\Theta$,
define the nonnegative set function
$$Q_\theta(A):=\int_A\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)}\,P_0(dx), \qquad A\in\mathcal A,$$
where the ratio is assigned value $0$ on the $P_0$-null set
$\{p_{\theta^*}=0\}$. Write
$$q_\theta:=Q_\theta(\mathsf X) =\mathbb E_{P_0}\left[\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $q_\theta\ne1$, $Q_\theta$ is not a probability law. The local
sigma-finiteness lemma proves that it is a measure. The local product-measure
lemma then constructs $Q_\theta^n$ and proves its density relative to $P_0^n$
is $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$.
